name: Grace Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter for one of the big main contractors, on a hospital extension that's going to take three years. Officially I do partitions, ceilings and fire doors, but more and more I help the site engineer with setting out, which means marking where everything goes from the digital model. I get in at seven, check the plan on my phone, and I've got a laser scanner app that shows if the walls match the drawings. I spend half the day on my knees and half on a screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask it to read the drawing notes and list what I need for each floor, I use it to write my daily reports, and on Sundays I ask it questions about the setting-out course I want to take. It gets things wrong sometimes, so I check, but it's quicker than waiting for an engineer to call me back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit boring, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a useful tool but it's not magic, and anyone who said it was got carried away. I'd probably post a short thing online about how it helps with reports but still can't fit a fire door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing, because I already use it for what it's good at. I own a small flat with a lodger who covers a lot of the mortgage, and I've got about seven months of savings. I'd keep moving towards setting-out either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the setting-out course next spring like I planned and keep using the tools. Maybe buy a better laser scanner of my own, around a thousand, so I can take on private surveys. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit of a shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the appeal of setting-out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's where the brain bit of the trade is. If you mark a wall ten millimetres wrong, everyone after you suffers, so it matters. And it's easier on the knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone who'd lose out even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe some of the office staff on site. But nothing big.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool but not magic, and anyone who said it was got carried away. I'd post that it helps with reports but still can't fit a fire door.
S0.think: It changes almost nothing for her because she already uses AI for what it's good at. She owns a small flat with a lodger covering much of the mortgage and has about seven months of savings.
S0.do: Takes the setting-out course next spring as planned and keeps using the tools. Might buy her own laser scanner for about a thousand to take on private surveys.
S0.quote: If you mark a wall ten millimetres wrong, everyone after you suffers, so it matters.
S0.fieldNote: Grace is already on a path from hands-on carpentry towards setting-out and uses AI as a routine tool. A plateau doesn't touch her plans. She thinks in terms of precision and responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I'm planning for already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but a manageable one, and people should get stuck in early instead of complaining. I'd say firms should pay for the training. I'd also say some of the hype people are wrong and some of the doom people are wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm well placed. I'm in the middle of a jump from carpentry to setting-out, which is half digital, and I'm comfortable with the tools. The partition crews worry me, because a lot of that is repeat work that factories and machines can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course this winter instead of next spring, and ask the contractor to move me onto the engineering team full-time. I'd buy the scanner and start doing weekend surveys for small builders. And I'd keep the lodger, because that income is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to keep any hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. I like finishing a door frame and getting it bang on. But I'd let it go if it meant a longer career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the partition crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve, who's fifty-five and great with a screw gun but won't look at a phone. He's got a mortgage and two kids at college. I'd try to get him onto something, but I don't know what.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big but manageable change, and people should get stuck in early rather than complain, with firms paying for training. Both the hype and the doom crowd are partly wrong.
S1.think: She's well placed, midway through a jump from carpentry into the half-digital work of setting-out. She worries about partition crews, whose repeat work factories and machines could take.
S1.do: Brings her setting-out course forward to this winter and asks to join the engineering team full-time. Buys a scanner for weekend surveys for small builders and keeps the lodger.
S1.quote: I'd let it go if it meant a longer career.
S1.fieldNote: Grace speeds up her existing plan rather than making a new one. She's pragmatic about giving up hands-on work she enjoys. Her concern for an older colleague, Steve, is real but she has no answer for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that skips over my whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a serious plan from government and companies, now, for income and retraining, and I'd say it without panicking. I'd tell people on site to save what they can. I'd try to sound steady, because people would be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Setting-out is exactly what an AGI with a robot could do better than me, it's measuring and models. My move up the ladder would mean nothing if the ladder goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder straight away and put any spare into paying down the mortgage. I'd try to get on whatever team runs the robots on site, because someone has to check them at the start. And I'd rent out my second room too, so I'd have two lodgers and more cash coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than I'd want to admit at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, my head start doesn't help much. Being early only counts if there's time for it to pay off. In two years everyone ends up in the same boat, just a few months apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two lodgers means giving up your space. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rubbish, honestly. I bought the flat to have my own place. But I'd rather share my kitchen than lose the flat.

S2.say: I'd say we need a serious plan from government and companies now for income and retraining, and I'd say it calmly. I'd tell people on site to save what they can.
S2.think: She'd be worried, because setting-out is measurement and models, exactly what an AGI with a robot could do better. Her move up the ladder would mean nothing if the ladder disappeared.
S2.do: Saves harder at once and pays down the mortgage, and tries to join whichever team runs the robots on site. Rents out her second room for extra income.
S2.feel: Anxious, more than she'd admit at work.
S2.quote: My move up the ladder would mean nothing if the ladder goes.
S2.fieldNote: Grace's adaptability doesn't protect her here, and she knows it: the move she's making is towards highly automatable work. Owning the flat is her anchor, and she'd give up space to keep it. She'd perform steadiness for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Some room to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, so firms and governments should get training going. I'd say workers should learn to work with the robots, not wait for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me ride the wave a bit. I'd get into setting-out, then into checking robot work, then maybe managing a site, and I'd have built up savings. At thirty-two, I'd still be adaptable, but I don't know what I'd adapt to at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd finish the setting-out course and learn the robot setting-out systems the big firms are testing. I'd keep the lodger, pay the mortgage down faster and build my survey business on weekends. I'd look at site management qualifications around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel busy and mostly in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you hope to be when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owning my flat outright, with a couple of years of savings, and in a role where I'm responsible for a site. Whether that role survives, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still recommend carpentry to a sixteen-year-old?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture? I'd say learn it, but learn the computer side too. Carpentry teaches you how things fit together, and that doesn't go out of date.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, with firms and governments getting training going. Workers should learn to work with robots, not wait for them.
S3.think: Five years lets her ride the wave from setting-out to checking robot work to site management, building savings as she goes. At 32 she'd still be adaptable but unsure what she'd adapt to.
S3.do: Finishes the setting-out course this year and learns the robotic setting-out systems big firms are testing. Pays down the mortgage faster, grows her weekend survey business and looks at site management qualifications around year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy and mostly in control.
S3.quote: Carpentry teaches you how things fit together, and that doesn't go out of date.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Grace builds a staircase of roles and savings. She's honest that the final step is uncertain. Owning her flat outright is her clearest goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's real time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to get caught out. Government and companies should set up training now, and people should take it. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for most of it. I'd move up to site management, pay off the flat, maybe buy a second one to rent. The end point still makes me uneasy, because if machines do almost everything, I don't know what a site manager does either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do setting-out now, site management in a few years and start my own small survey business on the side. I'd invest in a second property around year five. And I'd keep learning each new tool as it comes, the same way I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why property, rather than shares or more training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I understand buildings. I can see a flat and know what needs doing. Shares feel like gambling to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade change who you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it gives Steve time to retire. He'd be sixty-five. That's the one bit where the slow version is really kinder.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, so nobody has an excuse to get caught out. Government and companies should set up training now and people should take it.
S4.think: She'd be fine for most of the decade, moving into site management, paying off her flat and maybe buying another to rent. The end point still unsettles her because she can't see what a site manager does either.
S4.do: Does setting-out now, site management in a few years and starts a small survey business on the side. Invests in a second property around year five and keeps learning each new tool.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, but sleeping fine.
S4.quote: Shares feel like gambling to me.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives Grace room for a full plan built on property and promotion. Her unease is about the end state rather than the path. She noticed that the slower picture lets her older colleague reach retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it overtakes everything I'm working towards before I get there. What would help is time-limited income support and proper training paid for by the companies that bring the machines in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be a woman in this trade who finally found her place. It took me years to be taken seriously on site. I'd hate for that to be undone by a robot that never had to prove itself.

headlineQuote: I'd hate for that to be undone by a robot that never had to prove itself.
portrait: Grace Kowalski is a 27-year-old carpenter on a hospital extension for a big contractor, moving into setting-out and using AI every day. She owns a small flat with a lodger and has about seven months of savings. She's calm in the mild pictures, already accelerating her plans, but the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because the work she's moving into is exactly what AGI could do. With more time she plans a ladder of roles, a survey business and property, while worrying about older colleagues like Steve.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would overtake everything she's working towards before she gets there.
whatWouldHelp: Time-limited income support and proper training paid for by the companies that bring the machines in.
